summary: Describes RANGER, an architectural framework for scalable routing and addressing in networks with global enterprise recursion. An "enterprise" here can range from a small home office network to a multi-organizational corporation, or even the global Internet itself, and the framework nests them. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Networks can sit inside bigger networks like nested boxes. RANGER is a plan for how addresses and directions can work across all of the boxes while the whole Internet keeps growing.

questions: how can routing scale with enterprise networks
what is the difference between an eid and an rloc
subtitle: An architecture for scaling routing and addressing by nesting networks inside networks, all the way up to the global Internet.

tldr.problem: Internet routing tables may not scale over the long term, IPv4 address space is running out, and enterprises with overlapping private addresses need a coherent plan for routing, mobility, multihoming and security.
tldr.mechanism: RANGER separates edge addresses (EIDs) from routing addresses (RLOCs) and uses automatic tunnels between border routers, with each enterprise nested inside a parent enterprise in a recursive structure.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational architecture framework from an Independent Submission, not a standard. It describes how VET, SEAL and ISATAP fit together rather than defining new protocol details itself.

today: RFC 5720 is an Informational document published through the Independent Submission stream, so it is not an Internet Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. The RFC Editor states it makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: What RANGER Is For
sections.content:
RANGER (Routing and Addressing in Networks with Global Enterprise Recursion) is an architectural framework for scalable routing and addressing. An enterprise here can be as small as a Small Office, Home Office (SOHO) network, as dynamic as a Mobile Ad Hoc Network, as complex as a multi-organizational corporation, or as large as the global Internet itself.

Such networks need a coordinated plan for routing and addressing with room for scalability, provider-independence, mobility, multihoming and security. RANGER also offers a framework for IPv6/IPv4 coexistence. It is manifested through composite technologies: Virtual Enterprise Traversal (VET), the Subnetwork Encapsulation and Adaptation Layer (SEAL) and the Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP), with mechanisms such as IPsec in scope for some scenarios.

The document mainly uses IPv6 as a virtual overlay over IPv4 as its example, but says the same principles apply to any combination of IPvX overlays over IPvY networks.
sections.eli5: RANGER is a big-picture plan for keeping the addresses and directions of many nested networks tidy, from a tiny home network up to the whole Internet.

sections.title: Key Terms: RLOC, EID and the Commons
sections.content:
The architecture rests on two kinds of address. A Routing Locator (RLOC) is an IPv4 or IPv6 address assigned to an interface in an enterprise-interior routing region. Private-use addresses are local to each enterprise, so the same ones can appear in disjoint enterprises. An Endpoint Interface iDentifier (EID) is an address assigned to an edge network interface of an end system. EID space must be separate and distinct from any RLOC space.

A commons is an enterprise-interior routing region where border routers of diverse organizations, possibly with competing interests, peer cooperatively. The Default-Free Zone of the global Internet is the prime example. A site is a grouping of interfaces whose topology is a proper subset of the enterprise, and sites can contain interior sites recursively.

Two router roles matter. An Enterprise Border Router (EBR) sits at the edge of an enterprise and is a tunnel endpoint in an overlay network. An Enterprise Border Gateway (EBG) is an EBR that also connects the enterprise to provider networks or the global Internet, typically acts as a default router in the overlay, and is synonymous with the term "default mapper". Tunnels run from an Ingress Tunnel Endpoint (ITE) to an Egress Tunnel Endpoint (ETE).
sections.eli5: Think of two kinds of addresses: a street address that only matters for getting around town (RLOC), and a name tag on a person's door (EID). Border guards at each town's gate translate between them.

sections.title: Map-and-Encaps and Enterprise Recursion
sections.content:
RANGER scales routing with an approach that parallels the scheme in RFC 1955, also known as map-and-encaps. An ITE that must forward a packet first consults a mapping system to find the RLOC of the ETE for the destination EID. It then encapsulates the inner packet in an outer IP header and sends it across the commons. The ETE decapsulates it and forwards it toward the final destination. As a result, the routing table inside the commons only needs state about RLOCs, not EIDs.

The mapping system is typically a per-enterprise distributed database kept in sync among a limited set of mapping agents, for example a routing protocol instance run by EBGs or a DNS reverse zone spread over a restricted set of caching servers. An ITE can query it itself, delaying or dropping initial packets, or send initial packets to an EBG acting as a default mapper.

The second idea is recursion. Large enterprises may run BGP internally across many internal Autonomous Systems, so one enterprise can look like an internet of its own, with default routes leading to the true global Internet. Each internal AS can in turn look like a lower-tier enterprise. This enterprise-within-enterprise framework can be nested as deeply as desired. Seen from the top, the global Internet is just one more enterprise, and the RFC even floats the idea that other internets could be joined as "parallel universes" at higher levels of recursion.
sections.eli5: Imagine nested boxes of towns. Each town keeps a small address book saying which gate to use for each person, so the big roads only need to know about the gates, not every person.

sections.title: How VET and SEAL Do the Work
sections.content:
RANGER is built on overlay networks created by Virtual Enterprise Traversal (VET), which uses automatic IP-in-IP tunneling. For each enterprise it connects to, an EBR configures a Non-Broadcast, Multiple Access (NBMA) interface called a VET interface, which sees all other EBRs in that enterprise as potential single-hop neighbors. Standard neighbor discovery such as router advertisements and redirects can then be used between EBR pairs, giving a data-driven model where neighbor relationships form from traffic demand. When a path crosses several VET interfaces, packets are decapsulated and re-encapsulated at each one.

EID prefixes can be provider-independent (PI), owned by the EBR, or provider-aggregated (PA), delegated by an EBG. The preferred way to sub-delegate PA prefixes down the hierarchy is DHCP Prefix Delegation (RFC 3633). A PI owner registers its prefix by sending Router Advertisement messages to EBGs, optionally signed with SEcure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971), and must send further RAs periodically to refresh expiration timers.

Routes can be found by running a dynamic routing protocol over the VET interface, by on-demand mapping lookups, or both. In the RFC's example, a router first forwards via default routes, then learns from an ICMPv6 redirect that a more direct next hop exists, proves it may send from the source prefix with an RA, and sends later packets directly.

SEAL gives each encapsulated packet an extended 32-bit Identification field (the SEAL_ID) that tunnel endpoints can use as a nonce to detect off-path spoofing. Endpoints using SEAL keep working even when many ICMP messages are lost, and can adapt to links with different MTUs. Using VET with SEAL is described as essential in certain deployments to avoid source address spoofing and black holes caused by path MTU limits.
sections.eli5: VET builds secret tunnels between the town gates, and SEAL stamps every package with a counter so a fake package sent by a trickster can be spotted.

sections.title: Legacy Services, Mobility and Multihoming
sections.content:
Legacy nodes already numbered with RLOC addresses need continued access to RLOC-based services, possibly indefinitely. The RFC lists options for reaching the legacy IPv4 Internet from nested enterprises: ordinary IPv4 forwarding with a NAT at the edge when all enterprises share one IPv4 RLOC space, a Carrier-Grade NAT reached by IPv4-in-IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling when they do not (avoiding a brittle stack of NATs within NATs), or IPv6/IPv4 translation.

For mobility, the RFC separates three cases. Nomadic enterprises and end systems may just accept renumbering. Mobile enterprises with PI prefixes can update the mapping system, and moving between lower tiers of a common parent may cause no change in the parent's mapping system, which dampens churn. Fast-moving systems with PA addresses may need a rendezvous service, and mechanisms such as Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) and the Host Identity Protocol (RFC 4423) can provide a stable identifier. The RFC uses an aircraft and a wireless handset as examples.

For multihoming, EBRs can discover multiple EBGs and use them for fault tolerance and load balancing as long as they register their PI prefixes with each one. The RFC also notes that mapping choices have trade-offs: queueing or dropping initial packets during a lookup can hurt some applications, which favors forwarding initial packets via a default mapper while the lookup proceeds.
sections.eli5: Old devices keep using the old roads, and moving or well-connected networks can tell the right gates where they are now or use several gates at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Enterprises in a commons cooperate but may have competing interests, so mechanisms that depend on feedback from routers on the path can be brittle or open to spoofing. Path MTU Discovery is the example: for IPv4 a common workaround is to disable it and allow fragmentation, while for IPv6 the typical mitigation is to discard ICMP messages with insufficient information or use the minimum IPv6 path MTU.

The RFC says that when VET and SEAL are used, EBGs can combine the 32-bit identification in the SEAL header with ingress filtering to check that a message came from a topologically correct enterprise, without needing cooperation from other enterprises. Tunnel-mode IPsec between EBGs can be added where on-path spoofing is a concern. It also states that RANGER does not itself address security considerations, but proposes a framework for specifications that do.
sections.eli5: Since anyone can write a fake return address on a package, RANGER adds counters and checks at the gates so fake packages are easier to catch.
